title: Career roadmap · Green Building Policy Advisor
summary: This pathway combines building science, sustainable design, energy and environmental regulation, urban policy, and evidence-based advice to governments, institutions and industry.

facts.Timeline assumption: This roadmap assumes the candidate is entering or completing a Ph.D. focused on sustainable buildings, building performance, energy, materials, climate resilience or a closely related area. A policy career can develop through research, government programmes, consulting, standards work and international organisations.

horizons.question: What can I enter now?
horizons.output: Building-science research + policy analysis + measurable energy/environmental performance evidence.

horizons.question: How should I specialise?
horizons.output: Specialise in building energy codes, embodied carbon, green-building standards, climate resilience or urban sustainability policy.

horizons.question: How should I evolve?
horizons.output: Lead policy programmes, standards development, research centres or national/state sustainable-building initiatives.

horizons.question: How can I remain relevant?
horizons.output: Become a senior policy authority connecting building regulation, climate targets, technology and large-scale implementation.

blocks.text: Evolve and stay relevant, 2035–2046

Move from individual-building analysis toward policy systems: codes, incentives, public procurement, retrofit programmes, disclosure, embodied carbon and climate adaptation. Keep technical modelling skills strong enough to test policy claims rather than relying only on policy documents.

blocks.text: PhD routes
The selected qualification is already doctoral level. Further research routes include:

The strongest long-term profile will connect technical building performance with regulation and implementation. A senior policy advisor should be able to evaluate energy codes, retrofit strategies, embodied carbon, climate risk, incentives and compliance systems, then translate technical evidence into practical government policy. International frameworks such as UNEP's buildings work and the IPCC's climate assessments can provide the broader policy context.
